synth.x: The synth works in Hz rather than note names. A handy trick: set Frequency to 440 Hz and use Shift to move in semitones.
Square wave plus an LFO on Frequency and lots of reverb makes a siren. It can also work as an octaver, and forum member Simeon built a musical feedback simulation with it.
Connect a Synth block straight to the output with a sine wave and tracking off.

i: Set the synth block to a 1K sine wave at -12 dB.
The Synth block is reference quality. I use it all the time to generate test tones. The output is spectrally purer than my $2000 Stanford Research Systems Synthesized Function Generator.

synth.x: The Synth block doesn't support Global blocks.

i: Max Loop Time sets the loop length in advance: when the first recording reaches it, the Record 2nd Press action happens automatically.
Overdub Level works like a "loop decay": below 0 dB older layers fade as you add new ones (at 0 dB they never fade, but can build up and clip).
Crossfade smooths the loop seam; Trim Start and Trim End adjust the loop points on the graph.
Playback Level and Dry Level balance the loop against your live playing; Low Cut and High Cut filter the playback only.
Before the Amp block
Changing amp models changes the sound of the running loop.
After the Amp block
The loop keeps the sound it was recorded with.

looper.x: Record a loop before the Amp block, then adjust amps, cabs and effects while it plays. Or record a loop at a gig and walk the room to hear your sound from the audience.
Switches with a secondary HOLD function trigger on release, which delays Record. Remove the HOLD function from those switches.
The loop is erased when you change presets unless Spillover is enabled in Setup, and both presets contain the Looper.

i: Loopers have unique hardware requirements, i.e. lots of memory. [...] you're unlikely to ever find a multi-effect that has the loop time and features as a dedicated looper.

looper.x: The Looper doesn't support Global blocks.

i: Frequency sets the split from 40 to 800 Hz; the ×10 multiplier extends it to 400 Hz–8 kHz.
Lo Level and Hi Level set each band's level on the left and right channels.
Lo Pan and Hi Pan place each band of each input anywhere in the stereo output.

crossover.x: Split highs and lows into two amps, popular for bass. The PLEXI BI-AMP factory preset (Axe-Fx) shows it, and Leon Todd's "5 Minute Tones - Distorted Bass" video walks through it.
The FM3 has no Crossover block: put two Filter blocks on parallel rows, one low-pass and one high-pass at the same frequency and default Q. See the POLYFUZZ CROSSOVER FM3 factory preset.
The forum thread "The Flint Tremolo Done Right" uses the Crossover to emulate a Strymon Flint-style harmonic tremolo.
The Crossover block doesn't support Global blocks.

i: Gain (0–100%) and Balance for each of rows 1–6.
A per-row delay of up to 64 samples (roughly 1.3 ms) for lining up parallel paths in time and phase. Added in firmware 32.01.
Mono/Stereo output, plus a master Output Level and Output Balance.

mixer.x: Attach an expression pedal or switch to the Mixer gains to use one pedal as a wah or a whammy, or to crossfade between two Amp blocks.
Use the per-row Delay to compensate for latency when routing in parallel, for example to outboard gear.

i: What I do is generate a sine wave with the Synth block, flip the polarity into the outboard gear and adjust the delay until they cancel out.

mixer.x: Output blocks have basic mixing controls of their own: the preset's overall level and the relative levels of the grid rows, per scene.
The Mixer can't be bypassed and doesn't support Global blocks.

i: Input Select chooses the active source; attach a modifier to switch it from a pedal or footswitch.
Input Mode: STEREO, LEFT or RIGHT only (sent to both outputs), or SUM L+R to mono.
Level and Balance; no Bypass.
If you want cross-fades between amps you would use two amps and the new Multiplexer block which cross-fades between input sources. You can set the input source to be any row or physical input.

mux.x: The forum thread "How to use the MUX to switch a single pedal between Wah and Whammy duties" shows a popular setup.
The Multiplexer can't be bypassed and doesn't support Global blocks.

sendreturn.x: Tap the main signal into, say, a Graphic EQ and a 100%-wet Delay, then send the delay's output back to the start of that chain with Send/Return. Each echo passes through the effects again, and Return Level sets how quickly it fades. Search the factory presets for "feedback loop".
Start with Return Level at 0% and raise it slowly. If you hear squealing or runaway feedback, turn it straight back down: an unstable loop can get dangerously loud.

Put a Send at the end of one chain and a Return, at 100%, at the start of another row to continue past the grid's 14 columns. The Blocks Guide shows a real 28-block preset built this way at just over 80% CPU.

i: The reason the default level for the Return Block is 0 is probably so that when you insert it, you don't need to fear screaming feedback.

The feedback return clips at a level of 38 dBu. This is nearly 10 times the maximum output level of the unit. If this protection were not there a feedback loop could be created that would result in digital overflow and cause a reboot.

sendreturn.x: Send/Return may add a little latency, and neither block supports Global blocks.

i: Filter Type (High Shelf, Low Shelf or Peaking) with Frequency, Q and Gain. The graph is drawn upside down compared with the effect on tone: a dip in the graph boosts the mids and a peak cuts them.
Clip Shape, from smooth to hard (more "brash"); Bias sets the balance of even and odd harmonics; Drive sets the overall amount.
Mono or Stereo processing, plus Level and Pan.

dynadist.x: Put it after delay or modulation effects to give them some vintage grit; see forum member Javajunkie's example linked from the wiki.

i: Analysis Source and Channel pick the "modulator" input, usually a mic; the carrier is whatever feeds the block on the grid.
Number of Bands, Min and Max Frequency, and Filter Resonance (Q) set up the filter banks.
Frequency Shift moves the carrier bands against the analysis bands for "anonymous mob informant" or "chipmunk" voices.
Freeze holds the current vowel; Highpass Mix lets consonants and air through for intelligibility; Attack and Decay set the envelope followers.
Master Level and Pan, plus Level and Pan for each of the 24 bands.

vocoder.x: The wiki links forum threads "Setting up the Vocoder block", "Vocoder - how to use?" and "Vocoder: the least used effect block?", and several video tutorials.
The Vocoder doesn't support Global blocks.

i: Decay Time: how slowly each band falls back on the display.
Input Select: watch the Left or Right channel alone, or both summed (L+R).
Bands: display resolution of 32, 64 or 128 bands.
Window Type: Hann or Blackman, the analyzer's window function.
Turn the Value knob to highlight a band (shown in red); its frequency appears in the upper left corner (firmware 1.13). Firmware 19.00 added y-axis labels.

rta.x: Highlight the band where feedback or a harsh peak shows up, read its frequency, and cut it with a Parametric EQ.

i: Use it to identify problem frequencies or as a spiffy screen saver.

rta.x: Set a Synth block to pink noise, send it out through an external EQ or pedal and back in, and watch the RTA to see that device's frequency response. The wiki also gives a step-by-step test of the Instrument input using a 1 kHz sine from the Synth block.
It also makes a good animated display on stage.

i: Place the block on the grid and press Edit. The current scene is shown at the top; use Scene - and + to move between scenes.
Each of the eight rows is one message. Type is PC (Program Change), CC (Control Change), or -- for an unused row.
Channel is the MIDI channel; Number is the CC number (for CC messages); Value is the PC number or CC value.
Clear Row empties the selected row for this scene; Test Row sends just that row so you can check it.

scenemidi.x: Scene 1 sends PC 11 on channel 3 and PC 64 on channel 4; Scene 2 sends PC 14 and PC 59 on the same channels.
Scene 1 sends CC 80 = 0 on channel 3 and CC 81 = 127 on channel 4; Scene 2 swaps the values, like flipping two toggle switches.
One scene can send a CC and a PC to the device on channel 9, while another sends nothing to it and talks to three other devices instead.
Because it only sends to MIDI OUT, it can't control the unit it's in directly. The wiki's workaround: connect MIDI OUT back to the unit's own MIDI IN.
Scene MIDI doesn't support Global blocks.

input.x: The Input block is the spot where the digitized audio signal enters the grid. The Axe-Fx, FM9 and FM3 have multiple inputs. The VP4 and AM4 have a single input (no block).
The Input block also provides these functions:

i: Gate/Expander block and input gate
Input impedance (not on FM3 and AX8)

input.x: On the Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3, the Input block can also operate as an effects return in an effects loop. See below.

i: An Input block cannot clip. All processing is floating point.
Active (not bypassed): the block ignores anything wired into it on the grid and always outputs its own input.
Bypassed: it acts like a shunt and passes along whatever reaches it on the grid.
Input blocks have four channels, so gate and level settings can change per scene.
Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3
The Input blocks can be positioned anywhere on the grid
Axe-Fx II , AX8 , FX8 , VP4 , AM4
The Input block is fixed at the start of the grid

input.x: The Input blocks are linked to the hardware analog input ports. See Audio I/O and amplification for more information.
The Setup menu on the Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3 allows inputs to be linked to digital input.
Additionally, the Axe-Fx III and FM9 have an Input USB block. This gets its input signal from USB Outputs 7+8 from a computer. It can be placed anywhere on the grid.
Note that the Multiplexer block can connect directly to a physical input port, without requiring an Input block in between.
There's a Level parameter in the Input block. This lets you adjust presets to the output level of a specific guitar. The parameter has a modifier, allowing adjustment per pedal or switch.
The impedance of the instrument ports on the devices:
Variable

i: Axe-Fx III (front)
FM9

input.x: Fixed (1 Megaohm)

i: FM3

input.x: Auto, or variable, input impedance changes the analog circuitry of the input jack to interact with the guitar pickup. In Auto mode, the impedance is set automatically, based on the first non-bypassed effect to follow the input. This simulates the way some classic effects “load down” pickups, causing a change in frequency response. Input impedance is also referred to as “Input Z”.
The FM3 and AX8 do not support auto input impedance.
Input impedance is in particular relevant when using fuzz pedals. Fuzz, buffers and impedance contains more information.
Forum member Sprint investigated which effect block types can trigger a change in impedance in “ Axe-Fx blocks that can influence Input Impedance ”.

i: Drives

input.x: BB Pre (230k) BB Pre AT (230k) Bender Fuzz (22k) Colortone Booster (90k) Colortone OD (90k) FaceFuzz (22k) FullOD (230k) Gauss Drive (230k) Master Fuzz (22k) OD One Overdrive (230k) Pi Fuzz (32k) Pi Fuzz - Ram's Head (32k) Pi Fuzz - Russian (32k) Pi Fuzz - Triangle (32k) Super Fuzz (32k) Super OD (230k) Treble Boost (70k)

i: Phasers

input.x: Classic Vibe (70k) Naughty Rock (90k)

Forum member Moke tells us we can get around the “1st active block in the chain” thing if needed, by putting any blocks in front of the Drive(s) that you want ignored, one row above. The algorithm only looks at blocks to the right of the Input block in the same row, or below, not above.

i: Some old stomp boxes, i.e. Univibe, fuzzes, etc. have a low input impedance. This low input impedance will load down a guitar's pickups and change the frequency response of the pickups. You cannot simulate the effect of pickup loading after signal acquisition since the pickup parameters are an unknown quantity. So if you want to exactly model one of these old stomp boxes you need to replicate the impedance loading. The 11R and the Axe-Fx II do this by switching in resistors and capacitors on the inputs that change the input impedance to match the device being modeled. I do not believe that input impedance affects feel in any way. This is simply impossible. I remember people saying they could feel the input "pushing back". Silly. It will, however, definitely affect the sound as the frequency response of the guitar will be altered. The resonant frequency of the pickups will shift…

The pickups see a load. That load is the impedance of the cable and the impedance of the amp input. The typical input impedance of a tube amp is a resistance plus a small capacitance to ground (120 pF or so). The Axe-Fx input simulates this input impedance. Some effect pedals present a different load. The Axe-Fx replicates this by switching in different load resistors and capacitors when a model of that effect is first in the effects chain.
It's not virtual. It physically switches in a capacitor.
You can simulate the effect of a guitar into a Fuzz-Face using the Input-Z feature.
You can use the Input Impedance control to lower the input impedance and flatten the response. Try 220K, that will be close to your passive DI.
The first block must be engaged for the impedance to change. If it is bypassed the impedance will revert to 1M.

Variable impedance is only used for pedal modeling. Tube amp models are always 1M (no capacitor). The reason it was not included in the FM3 was cost and space. The input impedance of the FM3 and Axe-Fx III without any additional resistance or capacitance modifications is identical and replicates the input impedance of a tube amp. Variable input impedance for our products is used only when modeling certain pedals. I can't speak for other products.
The front input has Auto-Z technology. The rear doesn't. If the preset/scene has a block that lowers the input impedance the inputs will sound different.

When you roll your guitar volume down you increase its output impedance dramatically. It can be upwards of 100K ohms. The self-noise of a 100K ohm resistor is quite high. Now amplify that (a lot) and you'll hear the noise. If you continue to roll the volume down you'll notice the noise goes away because the output impedance decreases.
It's not what the block sees, it's what your guitar sees. It's the load presented to the guitar. In this respect the hardware acts just like real pedals.

input.x: The Auto Impedance values are:
Auto 1MΩ 1MΩ + Capacitor. Use this to simulate a long guitar cable 230 kΩ 230 kΩ + Capacitor 90 kΩ 90 kΩ + Capacitor 70 kΩ 70 kΩ + Capacitor 32 kΩ 32 kΩ + Capacitor 22 kΩ 22 kΩ + Capacitor
Important: a buffered device before the instrument input disables the auto impedance feature. This includes pedals with buffers (such as BOSS pedals) and wireless transmitters.

i: A buffer will render the impedance stuff ineffective. It will also add (maybe considerable) noise which may defeat the low-noise advantage of the front input.
A wireless acts as a buffer. Hence changing the input impedance will not be able to load down the pickups.

input.x: Settings listed in the Blocks Guide: Auto (normally best), or a fixed 1 MΩ, 230 kΩ, 90 kΩ, 70 kΩ, 32 kΩ or 22 kΩ, each also available "+ Capacitor". It can be set per channel.
Engaging some effects, like Wah or Phaser, can cause a 'thump' in the audio. This may be caused by impedance switching. To solve this, change Input Impedance from Auto to 1M.
The above doesn't apply to Fractal Audio devices with fixed (not adjustable) input impedance (AX8, FM3).

i: The thump isn't the wah, it's the Input Impedance changing. If your preset is set to Auto for the Input Z, when you engage the wah the impedance switches. This causes a slight thump if you are playing since the load on your guitar changes. If you want to avoid this, turn Input Impedance to 1M OHM.

Set the Input-Z on the preset to 1M rather than Auto. The reason the Wah engages abruptly is because it switches the input impedance. Setting Input-Z to 1M overrides the impedance switch (and, frankly, sounds better IMO).

input.x: Each Input block has its own noise gate, and it processes whatever reaches the block, analog, digital or USB. From the Blocks Guide:

i: Mode: Easy shows fewer controls; Advanced shows them all.

Gate Type: Classic opens and closes like a gate pedal. Intelligent and Noise Reducer also filter out mains hum (match AC Line Frequency in Setup to your country's 50 or 60 Hz). Noise Reducer keeps the note attack and can let a little sound through; Classic and Intelligent can reach full silence.
Threshold: how quiet the signal must get before the gate closes. Turn it fully down to switch the gate off. The global Noisegate Offset in Setup shifts it for every preset.
Ratio: how much quieter the signal gets while closed; higher is more aggressive.
Attack and Release: how fast the gate opens (affects pick attack) and closes. Setting both very fast causes distortion.
Output Level: the level after the gate, handy for slamming an amp or effect.

input.x: For more on gating, see the Gate tab under Dynamics.
On the Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3, combining an Output block and Input block creates an Effects Send/Return loop. (see the Audio I/O tab)
The Input 1 block can be used with Global blocks (Axe-Fx only). The other Input blocks do not support this.

output.x: The Output block is the spot where the signal exits the grid and leaves the unit through the corresponding analog or digital output port.
The VP4 and AM4 do not have Output blocks.

There's an Output block for each physical mono or stereo output. Each Output block has 4 channels, and has a mixer with Level and Balance controls for each grid row, plus master Output Level, Balance and Bypass controls.

The Output block meters come BEFORE the Level controls (pre-fader) on the front panel, and are therefore uneffected by the Level controls. The meters indicate the internal signal level relative to full-scale (dBFS). When you hit the red line in the meters, you're still 12dB away from clipping.
The meters in the block are pre-fader (Level knobs on front of unit). The LEDs are post-fader. Simple as that.

On the Axe-Fx and FM9, the Output 1 block provides 20dBu output gain, even with the Level parameter at 0. This can be monitored by connecting the Input 1 block directly to the Output 1 block and looking at the meter in the Output block.
The Output blocks can be muted in SETUP > I/O > Audio. The signal is muted at the corresponding output AND on the grid.
The Output block level is stored per scene.

The Vol Inc and Vol Dec commands (footswitches and MIDI) provide a convenient way to adjust preset levels on the fly (without manual editing). They let you adjust the output level per scene in steps of 1 dB while playing. (see Vol Inc and Vol Dec on the Presets tab)

i: Output 1
Transmits signal to the physical Output 1 jacks and to USB Inputs 1+2 on a connected computer
Output 2
Transmits signal to the physical Output 2 jacks and to USB Inputs 3+4 on a connected computer
Output 3
Transmits signal to the physical Output 3 jacks
Output 4
Transmits signal to the physical Output 4 jacks

output.x: The signal from the Output 1 block may also be transmitted to the digital outputs, if SPDIF/AES Out Source is set to Output 1.
The signal from the Output 1 block may also be transmitted to Output 2 port, if Output 2 Copy Output 1 is turned on and there's no Output 2 block on the grid.
The Output 2 block signal may also be transmitted through the digital outputs, if SPDIF/AES Out Source is set to Output 2.

i: Audio I/O and amplification
Setup menu
Preset level

output.x: Every Output block has a mixer channel for each row of the grid, plus a MAIN Level and Balance. The channels always match the grid rows, whatever row the Output block itself sits on and whether a row holds blocks, shunts or nothing.

The Blocks Guide's example: six rows (Filter, PEQ, Compressor, Synth, Delay, Reverb) feed Output 1, each with its own level (from -6 to +6 dB) and balance (from fully left to fully right), and MAIN at -2.2 dB. That lets you set the mix of parallel paths right at the output, without extra Mixer or Volume blocks.

i: Bypassing an Output block mutes it, both at the physical output and on the grid (its Bypass Mode is always Mute).
Output blocks have four channels, so their settings can change per scene.

Eight Scene Level parameters (added in Axe-Fx III firmware 1.12) cut or boost the output for each scene. Vol Inc and Vol Dec on a footswitch or MIDI CC change the current scene's Output 1 level in 1 dB steps and save the preset.
Axe-Fx Outputs 3/4, FM9 Output 3 and FM3 Output 2 can be set in Setup to copy Input 1 (a dry DI for re-amping); putting that Output block on the grid overrides it.
Axe-Fx II , AX8 , VP4 , AM4
The output section is fixed at the end of the grid
Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3
The Output blocks can be positioned freely on the grid

Product information: Routing flexibility is enhanced by unconstrained placement of input and output blocks anywhere in the routing grid. Want to insert different outboard devices at different parts of the signal path? No problem. Simultaneously process discrete stereo output for acoustic and electric guitars? Easy. Send stereo to front-of-house, plus a true “Wet-Dry-Wet” on stage while recording a DI for re-amping later? No problem! Each output pair also has its own dedicated front panel LEVEL knob for convenient control.

output.x: When engaged, the Copy Output process occurs before the Output Mode settings in SETUP are applied. So, Output 2 receives the stereo signal from Output 1 no matter what Output 1's mode setting happen to be. This allows you to have independent mode settings for Output 1 and Output 2.
the presence of an Output block (Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3) or an FXL block (AX8, Axe-Fx II) in a preset, always overrides the Copy Output setting in SETUP.
On the Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3, a combination of an Output block and Input block can operate as Effects Send/Return loop.
Output blocks don't support Global blocks .

globalblocks.x: Also, only Input 1 supports Global blocks, the other Input blocks do not.
You can read more in the Owner's Manual .
The wiki's pages for the Enhancer, Formant, Ring Modulator and Tone Match blocks also say those blocks don't support Global blocks, though they aren't in the list above.
Global block operations are accessible from the Tools page in the Layout menu, and in the editors. There are several operations associated with Global blocks:

i: Link To

Links the selected effect with a Global block. The Global block data is NOT loaded. Upon saving, the preset the Global block is saved. Any other presets linked to this Global block will load the Global block data upon recall
Load From
Loads data from a selected Global block but does NOT link the block
Link To and Load From

Links an effect to a Global block AND loads data from the Global block. Upon saving, the preset the Global block is saved. Any other presets linked to this Global block will load the Global block data upon recall
Unlink
Breaks the link between the current effect and Global blocks
Unlink All Blocks From Global
Breaks the link of all blocks with Global blocks

globalblocks.x: After adding or editing a Global block, the preset needs to be saved.

If you've changed settings in one of the eight instances of a Global block, always save the preset first before loading another instance of that block, otherwise you'll lose your edits. In other words: you can not edit several instances of the Global block and then save the preset to save them all; you must save per instance .
To unlink a block from Global blocks, use any of these methods:
Axe-Fx III:

i: Use Layout > Tools on the hardware
Use the editor

globalblocks.x: Axe-Fx II:

i: Use the Global block menu on the hardware
Execute STRIP ALL GLOBAL DATA in SETUP
Press Enter in the Recall menu on the hardware
Use the editor

globalblocks.x: Modifiers are not included in Global blocks. When you link a block to an existing Global block instance, modifier settings will not be included/applied.
Workaround: copy and paste the block from another preset using the editor. This includes modifier settings.
Recalling a block from the Library also includes the modifier settings.
On the Axe-Fx II, you can also use Recall Effect on the hardware to copy modifiers from one preset to another.

There's no hardware or editor command to wipe all Global blocks and start from scratch. The only way to accomplish this, is to restore a backup of the factory system data, also known as a clean system file. Ask for this on the user forum.

To share a preset that contains Global blocks, you have to either send the system data file along with it, which is very unpractical, or unlink all Global blocks before exporting the preset to a file.
When using Fractal-Bot to create backups of presets that contain Global blocks, you need to backup the system data too, because that's where the Global blocks data is stored.
Alternatively, here's a method to save individual Global blocks:

i: Create a single preset with all your Global blocks.
Save that to backup preset slots.
In the first backup slot, set the blocks to global instance 1, unlink the globals and save the preset.
In the second backup slot, set selected blocks to global instance 2 (only the ones which use instance 2), unlink the globals and save the preset.
Repeat for subsequent blocks.

globalblocks.x: If something goes wrong and you need to restore an individual block or channel, just copy the block or channel from the appropriate backup preset, paste it into a preset with linked blocks using the correct global instance and save it.

When you've saved a block as a Global block, and you're going to dial in a channel of that block that hasn't been tweaked before, the channel's initial settings may be off. To make sure that everything is set to default, reset the channel or block before tweaking.
Be aware that when you use the editor to create a snapshot of a preset with Global blocks, the Global blocks data is not included in the snapshot.
Read Presets for a method to control the bypass state of effects blocks across presets.
The editors provide sort of a substitute for Global blocks. See Parameter Batch Set for more information.

New firmware brings new features to blocks. This can cause a parameter in a Global block to stick to its old value and become out of sync and not update across presets. To fix this, each preset that contains that Global block needs to be re-saved in order to update the preset to the latest revision. Luckily, FracTool or the Parameter Batch Set function in the editor (see above) make this easier; they allow you to automatically re-save presets, either all, or a specified number.

The system uses internal storage to save the Global blocks data. It's possible to exceed the available storage space when saving too many global blocks. In that case the system will no longer save additional Global blocks, or all values will be reset to minimum. So use them wisely.

modifiers.x: Internal controllers generate or manipulate a signal in real time, without the need to use a device like a pedal or switch. It's the system that does the work, not you.
An internal controller is assigned to an effect parameter through the modifier menu, see above.

Each internal controller can be configured per preset. Some of the ambient blocks, such as the Multitap Delay block , also have specific internal controllers of their own. Like an envelope follower on the input, which allows creating swell effects.
See the Owner's Manuals for information about internal controllers.

i: LFO
An LFO generates a signal as a familiar wave shape, or random signal. Each LFO generates two signals, A and B .

modifiers.x: The "Astable" LFO type simulates an astable Op-amp Multivibrator, commonly found in effect pedals.
The "Shape" parameter controls the LFO shape for all types except Square and Random. High values approach a square wave while low values approach a triangle wave.

i: You can start a sweep, ramp, etc. from a known value. When you stop the LFO it resets the function argument to zero. The output is then, for example, sin(0) = 0. The random type doesn't have a value associated with an argument of zero so it doesn't reset.
Sequencer
The Sequencer generates a pattern by looping through 2-32 stages, similar to a synthesizer.
ADSR
Similar to the Envelope follower, with ATTACK, DECAY, SUSTAIN and RELEASE parameters (thus ADSR ).
Attack
The time it takes to go from silence to maximum level
Decay
The time it takes to drop from maximum level to the sustain level or silence
Sustain
The volume of a note while holding it
Release
The time it takes to drop from the sustain level to silence after being released

modifiers.x: The "Type" control defaults to EXPONENTIAL. It's analog-style, where the ADSR has an exponential attack/decay. LINEAR selects a linear attack/decay.

i: Set the ADSR Mode to SUSTAIN and it will sustain at the Sustain Level until the input falls below the Threshold.
Envelope Follower

The Envelope Follower converts the input level to a signal, responding variably to playing dynamics. Play hard and the corresponding signal is loud. In comparison, the ADSR envelope generator always creates the same signal, but only triggers when you play hard enough (threshold).

modifiers.x: Use the Envelope Follower to create an Auto Wah: attach Envelope to the Control parameter in the Wah block and hit the note hard for more effect, and soft for less effect.

i: Pitch detector
The Pitch detector analyzes the pitch of your playing and puts out a low value for low notes and a high value for high notes. When not using Input 1, make sure to select the correct input.

modifiers.x: Pitch blocks in the Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3 and VP4 have dedicated pitch detectors of their own.
For more information, see these pages:

i: Add gain to higher notes
Use the sequencer to create a Slicer effect
In Various presets & tricks Bakerman explains how to expand the use of ADSR, generate auto-wah effects and remove pick attack.

modifiers.x: External controllers are gateways between devices like expression pedals or external switches, and effect parameters. You rock the pedal or press the switch, and the corresponding data affects the parameter value and the sound.
External controllers are almost always used in conjunction with expression pedals and external switches, and MIDI. The Wah pedal described above is a good example.
The Axe-Fx III, FM3 and FM9 support 16 external controllers per preset. The VP4 and AM4 support 4.

i: Why assign use an external controller to a parameter when you can also assign a pedal or switch directly to that parameter?

Well, let's assume that you have 50 presets with a Wah, where your pedal is connected to PEDAL port 1 and assigned as such directly to the Wah's Control parameter in its modifier menu. If you need to swap that pedal to PEDAL port 2, you'd have to edit all 50 presets. Not if you had selected External Controller 1 as the source in the modifier menu. Because then you only would have had to change External Controller 1 to PEDAL 2. Global assignments for External Controllers are set on the External…
Use a switch to turn an effect on/off

A common practice is to use an external switch to turn an effect on or off. The switch is assigned to an External Controller. And that External Controller acts as the modifier source for the effect's Bypass parameter. The side-effect is that you can no longer engage or bypass that effect manually otherwise. The On/Off state is determined by the external controller, exclusively.
What if the pedal is not connected

When a pedal is assigned to a parameter using an external controller, the system must know what to do if that pedal is not connected. That's what the INITIAL VALUE parameter is for, in SETUP > MIDI/Remote. I.e., to make sure that the signal is not muted if the pedal controlling the output volume is NOT connected, set the external controller's initial state vale to 100%. Important: Initial Value settings apply only to external controllers, not to pedals that are connected directly to the device.
MIDI
External Controllers can be controlled through MIDI. On the Axe-Fx III, FM3, FM9, AM4 and VP4, the MIDI CCs are assignable in SETUP.

modifiers.x: On the Axe-Fx III, FM9 and FM3, 5 manual controllers are available in the Controllers block and/or Performance Pages.
They can be used as modifier sources for real-time manipulation of parameters from the front panel, without needing external devices.
This applies to:

i: FM3 , FM9 and FC controllers
AX8

modifiers.x: The VP4 and AM4 do not support Control Switches.

Instead of an internal or external controller, a virtual Control Switch (CS) can act as a modifier source. The CS itself is controlled through an onboard switch or switch on an FC controller (latching or momentary).
The Axe-Fx 3, FM3 and FM9 have 6 Control Switches ( CS ). The AX8 has two Control Switches.
Groups
Control Switches can be made part of a mutually exclusive group. This means that engaging one will bypass the others.
Control Switches and Scenes

The state of a CS is stored per scene: On , Off , or Last . Last , which is the default, leaves the switch state unchanged when you change to a scene with this setting. The per scene settings can be accessed from the CS PER SCENE page in the Controllers block.
MIDI

The Control Switches also let you transmit MIDI at will by pressing the switch when using an FC-6, FC-12, FM3 or FM9. This doesn't depend on a preset change or scene change. Up to four MIDI commands (PC or CC) can be transmitted. Read MIDI for more information.
Control Switches are documented in the Owners Manuals for the FC controllers and FM3, FM9, and AX8.
The modifier operates between the data from the internal or external controller and the effect parameter. The modifier menu provides several options to manipulate the signal.
What does Auto-Engage do

The Auto-Engage modifier parameter allows engaging and bypassing effects automatically. Example: rocking an expression pedal will engage a Wah block automatically without having to press a switch first, like an optical Wah pedal.
Configure Auto-Engage
You can make Auto-Engage kick in depending on the pedal's position, or the speed with which you rock it.
The Speed options engage the effect when the controller changes more than 5% in any 20 ms interval.

The Position options engage the effect when the controller value is 5% greater than or less than the Off Value (depending upon whether the Off Value is less than or greater than 50% respectively). For example, setting the Auto-Engage to SLOW SPD, will bypass the effect when the controller value is less than, say, 5% (default). To engage the effect the controller (foot pedal) must be moved more than 5% in a 20 ms interval. This requires that the pedal be moved somewhat rapidly and prevents the effect from engaging erroneously if the pedal droops. Setting the Auto-Engage to SPD POS will bypass the effect in the same manner, but the effect will engage when the controller exceeds 10% (5% + 5%) regardless of the rate of change.

i: The on value is 5% higher than the off value. This is by design. It's called hysteresis and it's a common technique used in many "bang-bang" controllers, i.e. thermostats. This is to prevent chatter at the threshold.

modifiers.x: Firmware 27.xx for the Axe-Fx III (and corresponding firmware for the FM3 and FM9) added activity sensing to directly connected pedals, FC pedals and external controllers. This stops Auto-Engage from engaging an effect if the pedal/controller is not connected. This prevents, for example, a Wah being engaged if Auto-Engage is on but no pedal is connected.

Forum member Bakerman: Both auto-engage types need to go into the off zone (determined by Off Value) to disengage. Position/speed really only changes the conditions to engage the block. "Speed" type requires a certain rate of change instead of simply reaching some value.
To turn an expression pedal into a virtual "toe switch": set OFF VAL to around 90% and Auto-Engage to Medium or Slow.
Use Auto-Engage with scenes

When switching scenes while the effect is still engaged, the effect will also be engaged in the new scene. In other words, an Auto-Engaged effect survives scene switching, even with Scene Revert set to ON.
Alternatives to Auto-Engage

Auto-engaging an effect may cause an hickup in the audio when engaging the effect, for example when using the Pitch block to create a Whammy effect. To avoid this, use modifier settings like these instead of Auto-Engage:

i: Auto-engage = off
Min = 100
Max = 0
Start = 60
Mid = 0
Slope = 100
Scale = 10
Offset = -100

modifiers.x: These settings pass the unmodified signal at the heel-down position and switch to 100% processed sound when moving the pedal while retaining the expression pedal's regular functionality. This only works with effects where the heel-down position sounds like the unmodified direct tone and that have a Mix parameter. This rules out the Wah block.
Another alternative: use the approach shown in the DEVY TOWNSEND factory preset, where the hiccup when engaging is avoided using a Volume block.
This modifier parameter determines whether a modified parameter will be reset to its stored value when switching presets, or stay at its current value ( survive preset switching).

For example, you have an expression pedal assigned to a Level parameter. You set the pedal halfway and then switch presets. PC RST determines whether the new preset maintains the pedal position and sets Level accordingly, or sets Level at the stored value of the preset, regardless of the pedal's position. If it's ON, the stored value will be used, until the pedal is moved.

i: […] The new value must be 5% different than the previous value, otherwise whatever value the pedal is at, will immediately override the "PC RST" value. The idea is that the parameter is set to a value when you recall the patch. You then have to move your pedal a bit (5%) to regain control of the parameter. This is done for two reasons: Many MIDI controllers send the state of their expression pedals along with the PC message. If the behavior weren't as described, the stored parameter value wouldn't stick. Many MIDI controllers have "noisy" expression pedals where the value tends to bounce around a little. This prevents the stored value from being lost.

modifiers.x: The Damping modifier parameter determines how long it takes to move the parameter between values.
Damping provides separate Attack (up) and Release (down) parameters. This means that damping up and down can be set at different times.
Options:

i: Exponential damping (default: classic damping style where the modifier value has an exponential attack/decay
Linear attack/decay

modifiers.x: This modifier parameter selects the rate at which the modifier updates the target parameter. For most applications, a slow rate is sufficient. That's always the case with external controllers.
Under some circumstances, a slow or medium rate combined with an internal controller may cause “zipper noise”. Increasing the rate will reduce the noise.
Higher update rates increase background CPU usage and should only be used when absolutely necessary.
Read the Owner's Manual for more information and diagrams.

i: SCALE
Applies gain to the modifier curve, allowing the user to create steeper or shallower curves (vertical). Use this to optimize your pedal.
OFFSET
Allows shifting the curve up or down the Y-axis.
SLOPE
Introduces an "S"-shaped curve.

modifiers.x: Turning up the Scale will ensure that the Control value reaches maximum even if the pedal doesn't.

i: Create a Whammy effect, reaching an octave at toe-down, with extra "play" at the top: Pitch CONTROL; SCALE 1.089; OFFSET 10.0 Make the Auto-Engage "bump" disppear (true bypass at heel-down): Pitch MIX; Start 40; Mid 100; End 55; Slope 0; Scale 10; Offset 100 Make a modifier go straight from MIN to MAX at toe-down: START 0; MID 0; MAX 60; SLOPE 0; SCALE 10; OFFSET -100 Create a Log taper in a modifier menu: set "Mid" in the modifier menu to 20%. Adjust the Slope to avoid the dead zone

modifiers.x: The Axe-Fx III allows two sources per modifier (dual source modifiers).
This is not supported on the FM3, FM9, AM4 and VP4.

Current firmware for the amp modelers lets you assign a controller to a parameter and apply that either to a single channel or to all channels of the effect block in the modifier menu. This allows flexible use of a modifier, especially across scenes. Note that you can only select "single" once, meaning that you can NOT assign a separate controller to each of the four channels.
The Control block itself has 4 channels on the Axe-Fx 3, FM3 and FM9.
On the VP4 and AM4, a modifier always applies to all channels of the block.
Using modifiers increases CPU usage slightly. For example, when you move a pedal which is assigned to a parameter, it'll send control data which will increase CPU usage temporarily.
Search the Factory presets page for controller to see examples of usage of an external and internal controllers.
To see if and which controllers are used in a preset, go to the Controllers block and scroll to the last tab page.

You can do the same in the software editor. Press Enter after selecting a controller on the Mods page to open its Modifier menu, except for CONTROL modifiers. Exit or Control will return from a modifier menu to the Mods menu.
Modifier settings and controller assignments are not saved with Global blocks .
The software editors do not allow typing values in the Min/Max fields of a modifier menu, for technical reasons. Use the mouse instead.

i: Mix

The blend of dry and effected sound. On most blocks dry and wet are each about 6 dB down at a 50% setting; Delay and most effects that aren't time-based behave differently. On the VP4 and AM4, time-based effects use a different curve so they sit better in front of an amp, so the same Mix number won't sound identical there.
Level
The block's overall output level.
Balance
Every block has left and right outputs; turning Balance one way makes the other side quieter, for both wet and dry.
Bypass
Switches the block on or off, and can be controlled by a modifier for remote or automatic bypassing.

common.x: What a block does when it's switched off. Each block offers only the modes that suit it.

i: Thru
Fully out of the circuit, exactly like a shunt: none of its settings affect the sound.
Mute
Silences everything, wet and dry.
Mute In
Mutes the block's input, so no new sound gets in, wet or dry, but tails keep ringing. Good for delays and reverbs in parallel.
Mute Out
Silences the output and cuts tails off immediately. The effect keeps running inside, so turning it back on you hear whatever it's doing at that moment.
Mute FX In

Mutes only the effect's input: the dry signal passes and tails decay naturally. Mix, Level and Balance still affect the dry signal while bypassed. Use this for delays and reverbs in series when you want spillover.
Mute FX Out
Silences the effect's output while the dry signal passes. The effect keeps running inside, and Mix, Level and Balance still affect the dry signal while bypassed.

common.x: Spillover means the trails of a delay or reverb keep ringing after you turn the effect off or change preset, scene or channel. The Compander in the Delay block can affect it.

Spillover between presets is turned on or off in SETUP, and needs some extra steps described in the Owner's Manuals. That setting only applies to changing presets, not to scenes, channels or bypassing blocks.

i: Global spillover settings only apply to preset changes. Spillover between scenes is, in general, desirable and controlled by the bypass mode and state of the various blocks.

common.x: If you set the effect level with Mix and Level, trails can change volume when you switch presets. Keep those fixed and set the effect level with Input Gain instead. The Multitap, Ten-Tap, Plex and Megatap Delay blocks also support spillover between presets in current firmware.
On the FM9 and FM3, gapless preset switching requires Spillover set to ALL. A running Looper survives a preset change only if both presets contain the Looper in the same mode.

Delay and reverb trails always ring out when you change scenes, depending on each block's Bypass Mode. Spillover can break when switching a block's channels if the two channels use very different algorithms, for example a Digital Delay in one and a Tape Delay in the other.

i: Spillover is in there but the "right" way to do it is to use scenes. If you stay within a preset and use channels and scenes the spillover is perfect.

common.x: The block's Bypass Mode decides whether trails ring out or are muted: Mute FX In (series) or Mute In (parallel) let them ring.

i: Input Select
Which part of a stereo input the effect processes: Left, Right, or both summed (L+R, the default). On the Megatap, Multitap and Plex Delay, Reverb and Rotary blocks.
Input Gain
How much signal feeds the effect, like an aux send on a mixer; it doesn't touch the dry signal. On the Delay, Megatap, Multitap, Ten-Tap and Plex Delay, Pitch, Resonator and Reverb blocks.
Global Mix

Lets the global Effects Mix setting in SETUP shift this block's Mix by up to ±50%, so you can make every preset wetter or drier for a room in one place. On the Chorus, Delay, Flanger, Megatap, Multitap, Phaser, Pitch, Plex Delay, Resonator, Reverb, Synth and Ten-Tap blocks.
Stereo Spread
Stereo width: 100% is hard-panned, 0% mono, -100% swapped, and values out to ±200% use psychoacoustic tricks to sound even wider.
Kill Dry
Takes the dry signal out of the block's output. In a parallel path, that lets Mix set how much effect you hear, rather than leaving Mix at 100% and using Level. Found mostly on time-based blocks.

common.x: Most people chain effects in series, like pedals. Running them in parallel opens other options. The Blocks Guide's example: with delay and reverb in series, the reverb is on both your playing and the echoes; in parallel, only your dry playing goes into the reverb, so the echoes come out without reverb. Kill Dry, Input Gain and Mute In are the controls that make parallel paths easy to set up.
All the modulation effects (chorus, flanger, phaser, tremolo, delays and so on) and the two LFO controllers share the same set of wave shapes:

i: Sine, Saw Up, Saw Down, Log, Exponential, Random
Fixed shapes; Duty has no effect on them.
Triangle, Square, Trapezoid
Duty changes the symmetry, from 0% to 100%, with 50% as the normal shape.
Astable
Doesn't use Duty; its Astable Beta parameter reshapes it instead.

common.x: When an LFO moves a delay time (chorus, flanger and the delay blocks), the pitch change follows the slope of the wave, not its value: a triangle sounds like a square wave looks, and a square wave gives only clicks unless it's smoothed with some damping.
Phase shifts the right (or B) LFO output against the left: 0° keeps them together, 180° makes them move in opposite directions, and anything in between is allowed. Phase has no effect on Random.

Every Tempo parameter (delay times, LFO rates and so on) picks from the same list of note values, in the order below. Beats is each value's length in quarter notes, worked out from the note value: 1 is a whole note (4 beats), "trip" is two-thirds as long (a triplet) and "dot" one and a half times as long. 2, 3 and 4 are 2, 3 and 4 whole notes, i.e. bars of 4/4.

i: Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3
Let you choose the input to which the tuner listens. You can also select ALL inputs
VP4 and AM4
Detects signals at the input

tuner.x: The signal can be muted when the tuner is engaged. Muting only applies to the analog outputs.
You can choose between muting the input or output. Muting the input allows delay and reverb trails to ring out when engaging the tuner.
On the Home screen press the Tuner soft-knob.
Only on the FM3: hold Tempo .
In the editor, press the Tuner button.

The Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3, AM4 and VP4 can automatically display the tuner when an expression pedal is at the heel down position, i.e. the value is less than 5%. The best use is to combine this with the pedal as a volume pedal, because, when you set your expression pedal to the heel down position, the tuner will automatically display.
Find the setting for this in Setup > MIDI/Remote > Other.
Fractal Audio's FC-6 and FC-12 foot controllers provide a dedicated tuner action and screen.

Scroll to TUNER CC in Setup and hit Enter. Click the switch on the footswitch that you want to assign the tuner to. Or configure it manually by assigning the tuner's MIDI CC to a switch on a MIDI controller. An external switch can also engage the tuner.
The default MIDI CC for the Tuner is 15 on the Axe-Fx II, AX8 and FX8. Keep it like this to avoid issues.
The Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3, VP4 and AM4 let you set the CC manually in Setup.
Certain MIDI foot controllers, like the Gordius, RJM and Liquid-Foot, can show a graphical tuner display that syncs with the Fractal Audio device. This requires that you:

i: Enable real-time MIDI SysEx communication on the Axe-Fx II (Setup) by setting it to TUNER or ALL
Use a suitable cable connection which allows full bi-directional MIDI communications

tuner.x: To work with the Axe-Fx III, FM9, FM3, AM4 or VP4, these controllers must either implement Fractal Audio's proprietary communications protocol for those devices and act as a client, or use real-time MIDI SysEx communication ( PDF ).

The DOWNTUNE parameter allows simplified tuning when tuning down one to four semitones. The display will read the natural name of the note, i.e. if tuning down one semitone, an Eb will read E. In addition any blocks that utilize pitch information will also be transposed accordingly.
Use the offsets below in the Tuner configuration for Peterson GTR Sweetened tuning, from the Gear Page's Strobostomp users: Do you tune your Guitar in EQU mode or GTR sweetened tuning ? discussion:
Use the offsets below in the Tuner configuration for Buzz Feiten sweetend tunings (BFTS).
Reference
The DISPLAY MODE parameter lets you switch between displaying all flats, all sharps or a mixture of sharps/flats for the displayed note name.
Use the neck pickup, turn down the tone control, then hit the string with your thump. This will decrease the impact of transients and harmonics.
With any tuner the rule of thumb is to use the neck pickup. The "fullest volume" is not necessary.
The tuner display may be a little slow right after powering up the device.

i: There are background tasks that run after boot. The tuner GUI thread can get starved if you are using a preset with high CPU usage during this period.

tuner.x: Put a tuner pedal on top of or next to the Fractal device, and feed it a signal by connecting to an unused OUT1 port or Phones port.
If the device is connected to a DAW which is not set to a 48kHz clock sample rate, the tuner settings may be off.
The Axe-Fx requires a 48 kHz clock. Anything else will screw up the calculations.
If the tuner doesn't appear, verify that the Tuner menu is set to display the first tab page.
Also, for third-party MIDI controllers, SEND REALTIME SYSEX must be enabled in Setup, and the Axe-Fx II, AX8 or FX8 MIDI CC must be set to its default.
Tuner changes listed in the Axe-Fx III release notes:

i: "All" added as a Tuner input source, summing every input.
Downtune (tune down one to four semitones and still see the "natural" note names; pitch-aware blocks follow) and Display Mode (flats, sharps or mixed).
Higher tuner sensitivity.
Tuner on Heel Down: a controller below 5% (typically your volume pedal) brings up the tuner automatically.
Clip warning on the mini-tuner when Input 1 clips.
With Mute set to Input, only the selected input source is muted.
New tuner algorithm, faster and more accurate.
Selectable tuner color theme.

scenes.x: Read about scenes in the official manuals .

Scenes are like snapshots of your traditional pedalboard at a particular moment, with effects on or off, and set to specific sounds. Scenes represent a single preset in 8 different states/variations (4 on the AM4 and VP4).
The routing (grid) is always the same across all scenes of a preset. There's no way to create, enable or disable scenes, they are always there. But:

i: The engaged/bypassed Bypass state (AKA on/off ) of each effect block can vary per scene
The selected Channel of each block can vary per scene
Each scene can have its own output level setting in the Output block
A limited number of Scene controllers allow parameter values to change between scenes
A scene can send MIDI commands through the Scene MIDI block
Control Switches can be set per scene
Scenes have individual titles

scenes.x: All in all, scenes are similar to an advanced switching system for a traditional pedalboard or 19" rack.
Spillover of delay and reverb trails is preserved better when switching between scenes than when switching presets.
The hardware display and the switch LED on compatible foot controllers show the currently active scene.
Warning: Scenes 2-7 may have all effect blocks engaged initially. This is by design. Watch out for loud bursts.
The FM3 and FM9 provide a zoomed display mode, where all 8 scenes are displayed in a large font for easy viewing.
Turn the B knob on the Home screen to switch between display modes.
In zoomed mode, use the cursor keys to switch between scenes. Use the value wheel and press Enter to switch presets. The zoomed display mode is not available on the Axe-Fx III.

The channel of an effect block is set per scene. For example, Delay in scene 1 can be set to channel A, while the same Delay in scene 2 is set to channel B. Note that using different types of Delay or Reverb in each state may impact spillover. Of course, you can still use two instances of effect blocks (instead or in addition to channels) in your presets. This lets you bypass/engage each instance per scene at the expense of CPU.
The editor's Scene Manager displays an overview of all channels per scene.

i: Channels can be thought of as a preset for an individual block. For example, you can think of the Delay block as being a stand-alone delay pedal (or rackmount processor) with four presets. Scenes store the bypass state and channel for each block. By using scenes and channels you can use a single preset for an entire song, an entire set or even the entire show. Since the routing doesn't need to change things switch fast and smooth. When switching presets the processor has to assume the routing might have changed and therefore has to clear all the buffers, mute the audio, etc. which takes time and interrupts the audio.

scenes.x: Axe-Fx III

i: Use NAV up/down buttons on the Home screen
Use soft knob A in certain screens
Use an FC controller, another type of foot controller or a directly connected switch
Use MIDI (assign CCs in SETUP
Use the editor
Use MIDI PC Mapping

VP4 and AM4

Use MIDI
Use the editor

i: Use NAV up/down buttons on the Home screen
Use soft knob A in certain screens
Use an onboard switch
Use an FC controller
Use MIDI
